title: The nucleus as a physical system
task: Use the nuclide labels to recover proton number, neutron number, isotope identity, and neutral-atom electron count.
scene: Your first morning on the Hill. The Theoretical Division hands you four nuclide labels with no explanation and expects you to pull the right quantity out of each one before anybody calculates anything.
question: Use the nuclide labels to recover proton number, neutron number, isotope identity, and neutral-atom electron count.
takeaway: A nuclide symbol is compact bookkeeping: the student must translate it into particle counts before using it.
why: Notation is only useful when each symbol is tied to a physical count. The atomic number Z is the proton count, and it fixes which element this is. The mass number A counts protons and neutrons together, so the neutron count is A minus Z — a subtraction, not a symbol on the label. Two atoms are isotopes of one element when Z is the same and A differs. And a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, which is why Z decides the chemistry as well as the identity.
assumes: an atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons around it

title: Isotopes and chemical identity
task: Decide which properties two isotopes should share and which can differ, and justify each choice from electrons versus nuclei.
scene: Chemistry and Metallurgy is being asked what it can and cannot deliver, and the answer turns on one fact about isotopes. Everything shipped here has both a chemical form and an isotopic composition.
question: Decide which properties two isotopes should share and which can differ, and justify each choice from electrons versus nuclei.
takeaway: Isotopes share an element’s electron structure but can differ strongly in nuclear behavior.
why: Isotopes of an element share the same proton count and nearly the same electron structure, so they form almost the same compounds and respond similarly to ordinary reagents. Nuclear behavior can differ dramatically because the neutron count changes the nucleus itself. Half-lives can therefore differ by orders of magnitude even when chemistry barely changes. Mass-sensitive instruments can distinguish isotopes because they respond to the nuclear-mass difference that ordinary chemistry mostly ignores. The useful distinction is simple: electrons dominate chemistry; the nucleus controls isotope identity and stability.
assumes: chemical bonding is done by electrons

title: Ionization and detector signals
task: Build the detector chain in causal order, then identify which stage would fail if the instrument recorded noise but no radiation response.
scene: The Physics Division cannot see a single neutron or alpha particle, and neither can anybody else. Everything the Hill will claim about cross sections, backgrounds and yields rests on a chain of conversions working in order.
question: Build the detector chain in causal order, then identify which stage would fail if the instrument recorded noise but no radiation response.
takeaway: A detector records a chain of physical conversions, so a believable signal requires every link to work.
why: A detector measures the consequences of an interaction, never the radiation itself. Energy has to be deposited in the sensitive material first — nothing downstream exists until that happens. That deposit sets free charge or light, which is the transducer step and the one that decides what the instrument is sensitive to at all. Electronics then collect and amplify a response too small to handle raw. The data system digitises and stores a pulse last. Get the chain wrong and you are measuring your own apparatus.
assumes: radiation deposits energy in whatever it passes through

title: Mass defect and binding energy
task: Estimate the total binding energy in MeV.
scene: A theorist at the blackboard wants a scale estimate before lunch: how tightly a medium-heavy nucleus is bound. The arithmetic is useful because it puts nuclear and chemical energies on very different scales without requiring any weapon-design details.
question: Estimate the total binding energy in MeV.
takeaway: Tiny changes in mass correspond to large nuclear energies.
why: A bound nucleus has less mass than its separated protons and neutrons. The difference corresponds to binding energy through mass-energy equivalence. Working in atomic mass units makes the scale easy to see: about 931 MeV corresponds to one atomic mass unit. Multiplying the small mass defect per nucleon by the number of nucleons gives a total binding energy around 1.5 GeV for this example. The important result is the energy scale, not a recipe for releasing it.
assumes: mass and energy are related by E = mc², with E the energy, m the mass and c the speed of light

title: Energy calibration across instruments
task: Arrange the four cards from earliest cause or prerequisite to latest result.
scene: A spectrum is on the bench and somebody has written particle energies along the bottom of it. Los Alamos is about to compare spectra taken on different instruments in different buildings.
question: Arrange the four cards from earliest cause or prerequisite to latest result.
takeaway: Calibration is a measured mapping, not a label pasted onto the x-axis.
why: The instrument never measured energy. It measured the size of electrical pulses, and the axis is a claim that a particular pulse size corresponds to a particular deposited energy. That claim has to be established before an unknown spectrum means anything, which fixes the order: spectra from known reference lines first, then the peak channel positions, then a fit that maps channel to energy. Only then can the calibration be applied to unknown peaks — and the uncertainty in the fit has to travel with it.
assumes: an instrument records something electrical, not the quantity you wanted

title: Two development paths at Los Alamos
task: Match each historical program description to the path it implied, focusing on research organization and evidence rather than device construction.
scene: Oppenheimer has asked the divisions to compare two historically competing development paths. The useful question for this lesson is not how either device was built, but how each path changed staffing, diagnostics, materials work, schedules, and technical risk.
question: Match each historical program description to the path it implied, focusing on research organization and evidence rather than device construction.
takeaway: Competing architectures can reorganize an entire research program even when the underlying scientific goal is the same.
why: Los Alamos initially pursued more than one weapon architecture because neither path was guaranteed. The gun-type route appeared more familiar to ordnance engineers; implosion demanded a much larger program in hydrodynamics, diagnostics, timing, materials, and manufacturing consistency. In 1944 measurements of reactor-produced plutonium changed the balance and made the plutonium gun route unacceptable. For a senior-level course, the important systems lesson is how one material measurement can redirect people, facilities, tests, and schedule—not the construction details of either device.
assumes: a chain reaction needs the material held together long enough to grow

title: Radioactive decay law
task: Estimate what remains after three half-lives, then explain why the answer is an expectation for a population rather than a clock for each nucleus.
scene: A tracer sample has been sitting through a six-hour shift and somebody needs to know what is left in it. Every count taken here is a count of something that has been decaying since it was made.
question: Estimate what remains after three half-lives, then explain why the answer is an expectation for a population rather than a clock for each nucleus.
takeaway: Half-life predicts how a population changes even though no individual decay time is predictable.
why: Decay is random for any single nucleus and predictable for a large population. After one half-life about half the original nuclei remain. After two, a quarter. After three, an eighth. That holds regardless of how many you started with, which is what makes decay usable as a clock and as a correction. A six-hour shift against a two-hour half-life is three halvings. So the shift length is part of the measurement, not a detail about when it was taken.
assumes: a half-life is the time for half of a large population to decay

title: Radiochemical tracers
task: Correct the tracer result for radioactive decay, then use the corrected signals to estimate chemical recovery.
scene: Chemistry and Metallurgy is running separations on quantities too small to weigh and needs to know how much is being lost. Every percent lost is weeks of production at Hanford.
question: Correct the tracer result for radioactive decay, then use the corrected signals to estimate chemical recovery.
takeaway: A tracer measures chemical recovery only after ordinary radioactive decay has been separated from process loss.
why: A tracer is a small amount of radioactive material that travels with the chemistry and reports where it went. That turns an invisible loss into a measurable fraction: yield is what came out over what went in. The correction that makes it honest is decay — the tracer has been decaying throughout the separation, so a raw count afterwards understates the recovery and flatters the loss. Both counts have to be corrected to the same moment before the ratio means anything.
assumes: a radioactive sample announces itself through its own radiation

title: Background measurement
task: Use the sample and background counts to decide whether the excess is credible, and identify which comparison would make the claim stronger.
scene: A weak sample has been counting for an hour and the question is whether it is emitting anything at all. This is where an experimental group either establishes a real signal or convinces itself of one.
question: Use the sample and background counts to decide whether the excess is credible, and identify which comparison would make the claim stronger.
takeaway: A weak radiation signal is a comparison against measured background, not simply a positive number on a counter.
why: A detector counts events with no sample present. Cosmic rays, natural activity in the walls and containers, and the electronics all contribute. Subtracting a background only means something if it was measured the same way as the sample. Same geometry, same shielding, same instrument, close enough in time that nothing has drifted. So the background is taken with the instrument you will use, not merely in the room you will use it in. An excess that follows the instrument to a clean room was never coming from the sample.
assumes: a detector records events even with no sample present

panel.title: The excess that would not go away
panel.hook: A sample has been counting about 40% above the rate recorded last week. The group wants to log it as a genuine activity increase. Before that goes in the book, the counting station has been put through a short series of checks.
panel.riddle: Something in this room is producing counts. What is it?

readings.name: Gross count rate, sample in place
readings.purpose: The total rate from everything the detector can see. It cannot separate the sample from anything else contributing.

readings.name: Rate with the sample removed
readings.purpose: What the station counts with nothing on the stage. If the excess survives here it was never coming from the sample.

readings.name: Effect of extra lead around the detector
readings.reference: external gamma sources are attenuated by roughly half
readings.purpose: Lead placed outside the detector attenuates radiation arriving from the room. It does nothing about a source already inside the shield.

readings.name: Counts with detector high voltage off
readings.purpose: With no bias the detector cannot multiply real events, so anything still counted is electrical. Silence here clears the amplifier chain and nothing else.

readings.name: Detector moved to a clean room, no sample
readings.purpose: Whether the excess travels with the hardware or stays with the location. This separates a contaminated instrument from a changed environment.

readings.name: Second identical detector, same room
readings.purpose: An independent instrument in the same place. A genuine change in the room should appear on both.

readings.name: Ten repeat measurements
readings.purpose: Whether the effect reproduces. A fluctuation does not survive repetition; a real cause does.

title: Reaction cross sections
task: Estimate the macroscopic cross section and the mean free path.
scene: The Physics Division needs to turn a microscopic cross section into a laboratory-scale distance. This is the bridge from an interaction probability for one nucleus to how far a particle typically travels through bulk material.
question: Estimate the macroscopic cross section and the mean free path.
takeaway: Microscopic cross section becomes a bulk interaction scale only after it is combined with number density.
why: A microscopic cross section has units of area and describes one target. A material contains many targets per unit volume, so multiplying number density by cross section gives a macroscopic interaction coefficient with units of inverse length. Its reciprocal is the mean free path. The calculation teaches a general transport idea used in detectors, shielding, reactors, and medical physics: a small microscopic probability can still matter when particles encounter enormous numbers of possible targets.
assumes: a cross section is expressed as an area

title: Poisson counting statistics
task: Estimate the fractional counting uncertainty, then decide whether doubling the run time is enough to cut that uncertainty in half.
scene: A counting run has finished with four hundred net events, and the team wants to know how precisely that total is known before spending more beam time. Material, detector hours, and shift coverage are all scarce.
question: Estimate the fractional counting uncertainty, then decide whether doubling the run time is enough to cut that uncertainty in half.
takeaway: Counting precision improves only with the square root of the number of detected events.
why: A repeat of the same counting run will not give exactly the same total. For Poisson counting, the typical fluctuation is about the square root of N, so fractional uncertainty is about one over that square root. Four hundred counts therefore gives about five percent. Cutting that to roughly two and a half percent requires about four times as many counts, not twice as many. That slow improvement is the planning lesson: longer runs buy precision, but with diminishing returns.
assumes: radioactive decays arrive at random

title: Analytical yield and purity
task: Close the material balance, then decide whether the 91% assay answers purity or recovery.
scene: A separation batch has returned with an impressive recovery number, but the report does not make clear whether the recovered material is chemically and radiologically clean. Downstream teams are about to treat one headline percentage as the whole story.
question: Close the material balance, then decide whether the 91% assay answers purity or recovery.
takeaway: Recovery and purity answer different questions; a trustworthy materials report needs both.
why: Several different quantities can hide behind a word like “yield.” Chemical recovery says what fraction of the target material was recovered. Purity asks how much of the recovered material is actually the desired species, and a radiochemical assay may answer yet another question. A batch can score well on one and poorly on another. The report therefore needs enough measurements to distinguish loss, contamination, and misidentification instead of letting one attractive percentage stand in for every kind of quality.
assumes: a report can be accurate and still answer the wrong question
why_this_format: The updated lesson is about not letting one attractive percentage stand in for every kind of quality. A BALANCE forces the player to decide which readings belong in the material ledger and which do not; the 91% purity assay cannot close a recovery balance, while the vessel-wall loss can.
player_does: read the batch input, measured product, discarded-stream loss, wall-swab result, and purity assay
choose which readings count as material streams in the recovery ledger
add the previously uncounted wall loss and test whether the ledger closes within tolerance
trap_is_satisfied_by: The obvious measured product plus discarded stream accounts for only 93.9% of the input. Adding the 5.8% vessel-wall loss brings the ledger to 99.7%, within a 0.5% balance tolerance; treating the 91% purity assay as a recovery stream fails categorically.

streams.label: Measured product stream
streams.note: Derived from the panel: 93.9% in measured outputs minus 0.4% in the discarded aqueous stream.

streams.label: Target recovered from vessel-wall swab
streams.note: Not included in the measured process-stream total.

streams.label: Target-isotope fraction in product
streams.note: This is composition (purity), not a material-flow term.

answerText: The recovery ledger closes only after the vessel-wall loss is counted: 93.5% product + 0.4% aqueous loss + 5.8% on the walls = 99.7%, consistent with the 100% input within the stated balance tolerance. The 91% assay is a purity measurement, not a recovery stream.

failure_feedback.action: counting the 91% purity assay as a material-balance stream
failure_feedback.consequence: the ledger mixes composition with recovered quantity and can appear reassuring without accounting for the missing material
failure_feedback.line: That percentage tells me what the product is, not where the material went.

title: Neutron energy and moderation
task: Match each neutron-physics question to the process that answers it: slowing, scattering, absorption, or detection.
scene: A neutron leaving a fission event carries a great deal of energy, and what happens next depends entirely on what it hits. Confusing the possibilities is how a shielding calculation goes quietly wrong.
question: Match each neutron-physics question to the process that answers it: slowing, scattering, absorption, or detection.
takeaway: Changing a neutron’s energy, changing its direction, and removing it are different physical processes.
why: Slowing, redirecting and absorbing are three different processes with three different consequences. In elastic scattering the neutron transfers some energy and continues as a neutron — it is still in the system. In absorption it is captured into a compound nucleus and is gone. Scattering off a heavy nucleus changes direction and gives up very little energy, because a heavy target barely recoils. Scattering off light nuclei is what slows neutrons efficiently, because a light nucleus can take a large share of the energy in one collision.
assumes: a light ball loses more energy hitting something its own size

title: Neutron detection
task: Hold the source and geometry fixed. Change only the discriminator threshold, read the count rate, then return the threshold to its starting state.
scene: A neutron counter is reading well below prediction and nobody yet knows whether the physics or the instrument is at fault. The measurement about to be built on this counter is one the whole plutonium programme depends on.
question: Hold the source and geometry fixed. Change only the discriminator threshold, read the count rate, then return the threshold to its starting state.
takeaway: A detector disagreement becomes scientific evidence only after efficiency, energy response, and calibration are checked.
why: A neutron carries no charge, so it cannot ionise a detector the way an alpha particle does. Every neutron detector works indirectly. It turns the neutron into something charged, or into light, or into a radioactive product counted later. Each conversion has its own efficiency and its own energy range. Each is a place a count can be lost with nothing looking broken. So before believing a low number, find one measurement that does not go through the same electronics. A threshold set too high loses real events silently.
assumes: a detector responds to charge, and a neutron carries none
why_this_format: The panel already shows that neutrons are arriving and that pulses are piling up just below the discriminator. CONTROL makes the player isolate the suspected setting instead of merely naming it: hold the certified source and geometry fixed, move one threshold, observe the rate change, then reverse the change to show that the effect follows the setting.
player_does: lock the certified source and source-detector geometry
move only the discriminator from its current high setting to the calibrated setting and read the count rate
return the discriminator to the high setting and confirm that the lost counts return with it
trap_is_satisfied_by: The count-rate response is about 860 counts/min (340 to about 1,200) while the repeat-run noise is about 60 counts/min from the panel’s 5% scatter. The response is therefore more than 14 times the noise, comfortably above the required 3× separation.

independentCheck.label: Activation foil at detector face
independentCheck.meaning: neutrons reached the detector face without using the counter electronics

answerText: With the source and geometry unchanged, moving only the discriminator to its calibrated setting restores the rate from 340 toward the expected 1,200 counts/min; returning the high threshold reproduces the loss. The independent activation foil already showed that the neutrons were arriving.

failure_feedback.action: changing the threshold and geometry together
failure_feedback.consequence: the count-rate change becomes ambiguous because two causes changed at once
failure_feedback.line: One change at a time, or the rate cannot tell us what fixed it.

title: The measurement that forced a program change
task: Put the historical evidence chain in order from the plutonium measurement to the Los Alamos program decision.
scene: Measurements of reactor-produced plutonium have returned from the counters, and Ordnance has been called in. The student’s job is to distinguish what the instruments established from the engineering decision that followed.
question: Put the historical evidence chain in order from the plutonium measurement to the Los Alamos program decision.
takeaway: A material measurement can invalidate an architecture without the measurement itself dictating every detail of the replacement.
why: Reactor-produced plutonium contained more plutonium-240 than the early program had assumed, increasing its spontaneous-neutron background. That observation undermined the viability of the plutonium gun concept and forced Los Alamos to concentrate on implosion. Keep the categories separate: the counters supplied a material fact; physicists interpreted its consequence for the existing program; managers then redirected people and facilities. The lesson is how evidence propagates through a technical organization, not how to reproduce the device.
assumes: a chain reaction started early releases energy early

dayTitle: Recognize when evidence forces a pivot
title: Expected events in a measurement gate
task: Use rate × time to compare how many spontaneous events a detector expects in a long gate and a gate one thousand times shorter.
scene: A source on the bench produces spontaneous neutron events at a steady average rate. The counting group is comparing two electronic observation gates, one a thousand times shorter than the other, to see how the expected background scales.
question: Use rate × time to compare how many spontaneous events a detector expects in a long gate and a gate one thousand times shorter.
takeaway: For a steady random source, the expected number of events scales directly with the length of the observation window.
why: If events arrive at an average rate R, a time window t contains an expected count λ = Rt. That is a general counting result used throughout experimental physics. A shorter gate does not change the source; it changes how much background the instrument admits. The actual count still fluctuates because the events are random, but the expectation scales linearly with time. Use this scene to practice event-rate reasoning at a detector bench, then carry only the qualitative lesson—that timing can change vulnerability to a background—into the historical discussion.
assumes: some heavy nuclei split without being hit by anything

dayTitle: Recognize when evidence forces a pivot
title: Why Thin Man was abandoned
task: Arrange the evidence chain from the new plutonium measurement to the historical program decision, without adding design details the measurement did not establish.
scene: Thin Man was the early plutonium gun program. In 1944, measurements of reactor-produced plutonium returned a result that contradicted one of that program’s core assumptions, and the laboratory reorganized rapidly.
question: Arrange the evidence chain from the new plutonium measurement to the historical program decision, without adding design details the measurement did not establish.
takeaway: A program pivot is strongest when the chain from observation to interpretation to decision is explicit.
why: The historical sequence starts with an unexpectedly high spontaneous-neutron background in reactor-produced plutonium. Physicists then recognized that the result invalidated a key assumption of the plutonium gun program. That produced the technical conclusion that the route was unacceptable for that material, after which Los Alamos concentrated its plutonium effort on implosion. Notice the categories: measurement, interpretation, technical conclusion, program decision. Keeping them separate makes the history more rigorous and models how senior scientists should argue when one new result overturns a large body of work.
assumes: a measurement can rule out a design without anybody being wrong

dayTitle: Recognize when evidence forces a pivot
title: Turn a pivot into a research program
task: Arrange the program-building steps from defining the new problem to producing evidence that can support an integrated decision.
scene: The old plutonium path has been stopped. Oppenheimer now has to turn the alternative from a difficult concept into a coordinated research program without pretending that choosing the direction has proved it will work.
question: Arrange the program-building steps from defining the new problem to producing evidence that can support an integrated decision.
takeaway: Choosing a new architecture begins a new evidence program; it does not end uncertainty.
why: A responsible pivot starts by naming the requirement the old path failed and the observables the replacement must satisfy. Then the laboratory builds non-nuclear experiments and diagnostics capable of measuring those observables, assigns interfaces across theory, materials, instrumentation, and manufacturing, and sets decision points where evidence can stop or redirect the work again. This is the systems-engineering lesson of the 1944 reorganization. The replacement program became dominant because it accumulated evidence, not because the word “implosion” by itself solved the physics.
assumes: a detonation travels outward from where it starts

title: Equations of state
task: Estimate the work scale.
scene: A high-pressure materials group is estimating the work done on a small sample in a press. The calculation is deliberately generic: its purpose is unit discipline and thermodynamic scale, not a model of a weapon component.
question: Estimate the work scale.
takeaway: Extreme-state calculations require both thermodynamic relationships and careful unit scaling.
why: An equation of state links pressure, density, temperature, and internal energy for a material. The familiar room-condition values may fail under extreme pressure, which is why direct measurements and careful models matter. For this estimate, pressure in pascals multiplied by a volume change in cubic metres gives joules. The calculation teaches scale and unit handling; it does not establish how a complex dynamic compression system behaves, because path, rate, phase changes, and nonuniformity can all matter.
assumes: pressure times a volume change is work

title: Phase diagrams
task: Use composition, temperature, and the observed microstructure to decide whether the phase diagram, the sample history, or the measurement itself deserves the next check.
scene: A metallurgist has a microstructure under the microscope that the phase diagram says should not be there. Everything the laboratory does with this metal is an argument with a diagram drawn from very little data.
question: Use composition, temperature, and the observed microstructure to decide whether the phase diagram, the sample history, or the measurement itself deserves the next check.
takeaway: A phase diagram is an equilibrium map; a real sample also carries processing history, kinetics, and measurement uncertainty.
why: A phase diagram maps which solid and liquid phases are stable at each temperature and composition. Crossing a boundary can melt a material, throw out a second phase, or change how it behaves under load. Plutonium is notorious for it. Several solid phases, and large volume changes between them. But a diagram describes one composition. So before doubting the map, check you still have the material it was drawn for. A trace impurity is enough to hold open a phase that should not be there.
assumes: a metal can exist in more than one solid form

panel.title: A phase that should not be there
panel.hook: A cast part has come back from metallography with two phases where the diagram says there should be one at this composition and temperature. It is measurably harder than the last five castings. The diagram is not wrong, so something about this casting is not what was assumed.
panel.riddle: The equilibrium map does not predict this structure. What did the metal experience that the map does not describe?

readings.name: Etched microstructure
readings.reference: single phase at this composition and temperature
readings.purpose: What structure is actually present. It shows that equilibrium was not reached or not what was assumed, without saying which.

readings.name: Bulk hardness
readings.purpose: A bulk mechanical consequence of structure. Many different second phases raise hardness, so it confirms the structure is real but does not identify it.

readings.name: Bulk composition assay
readings.purpose: Whether the alloy sits where the drawing says on the diagram. On-specification composition removes the simplest explanation for landing in a different phase field.

readings.name: Thermocouple cooling record
readings.purpose: How fast the casting actually cooled. Cooling rate decides whether the metal had time to reach the structure the diagram predicts.

readings.name: X-ray diffraction phase identification
readings.observed: a second equilibrium phase, not a metastable one
readings.purpose: Identifies which phases are present by crystal structure. It distinguishes a phase frozen in by fast cooling from one that is genuinely stable under these conditions.

readings.name: Trace element assay
readings.observed: one trace element at 9x its usual level
readings.purpose: Elements too dilute to appear in the major assay. Small amounts can shift phase boundaries or concentrate locally during freezing.

readings.name: Re-prepared and re-etched specimen
readings.purpose: Whether the feature survives new preparation. Polishing and etching can create appearances that are not in the metal.

title: What wavefront shaping means
task: Match each wavefront-control problem to the measurement or conceptual response that addresses it, using an optical/acoustic analogy rather than construction details.
scene: The mathematics group is using light and sound analogies to discuss how a front can change shape when different paths propagate at different speeds. The analogy is useful only if experiments measure the resulting front instead of trusting the sketch.
question: Match each wavefront-control problem to the measurement or conceptual response that addresses it, using an optical/acoustic analogy rather than construction details.
takeaway: Wavefront control is a propagation problem: different path times can reshape a front, but only measurement can show what actually arrived.
why: A wavefront can change shape when different parts of it travel through regions with different propagation speeds or path lengths. Optics gives a familiar analogy, and acoustics provides a safe experimental one: phase delays across an aperture can turn a flat front into a curved one. The historical implosion program confronted a much more nonlinear version of that general problem. For this course, the valuable physics is travel time, interface effects, manufacturing variation, and measurement—not the geometry or material recipe of an explosive lens.
assumes: a lens bends light by slowing it in some places more than others

title: How many half-lives have passed
task: Use the supplied values and give a sensible rounded result with units.
scene: A sample counted at 8,000 counts a minute reads 500 today, and the notebook does not say how long ago the first count was taken. The half-life is on the chart at 12 hours.
question: Use the supplied values and give a sensible rounded result with units.
takeaway: Exponential decay is counted in half-lives, and logarithms are how you get the number of them.
why: Every half-life halves the count rate, so the elapsed time is the number of halvings times the half-life. Eight thousand to five hundred is a factor of sixteen, and sixteen is two to the fourth: four half-lives, or 48 hours. Written as a logarithm it is log base two of the ratio, which is what a semi-log plot shows as a straight line. The useful habit is to work in ratios rather than differences — the difference of 7,500 counts means nothing on its own.
assumes: a half-life is the time for half of a sample to decay

title: Timing calibration
task: Read the whole reading panel, including the calm readings, then select the one cause that fits all of it.
scene: Four diagnostic channels see the same laboratory timing pulse at slightly different recorded times. The shared clock is healthy, but the individual paths are not yet calibrated. Until those offsets are measured, no later claim about physical simultaneity is defensible.
question: Read the whole reading panel, including the calm readings, then select the one cause that fits all of it.
takeaway: A common clock does not remove channel-specific delay; each path still needs calibration.
why: Every channel has to share one clock and have its own delays known. Cable length adds time. An electronic threshold shifts when a pulse is registered. A larger pulse crosses a threshold sooner than a smaller one even when the physical event was simultaneous. All of that is instrument, not physics — and the useful distinction is that a fixed error can be calibrated out, while a random one has to be engineered out. A channel with an uncalibrated delay produces a beautiful, repeatable, wrong answer.
assumes: an instrument adds its own delays to what it records

panel.title: Eight channels that will not agree
panel.hook: Eight channels watching one event report arrival times spread over 14 ns when the array is specified to 4. An independent clock cross-check came back clean, so the reference itself is sound. The spread is in the array.
panel.riddle: Every channel sees the same event. What is different about what each one reports?

readings.name: Channel-to-channel arrival spread
readings.purpose: How badly the array disagrees. It establishes that a problem exists without locating it.

readings.name: Independent clock cross-check
readings.purpose: Whether the shared time reference is where it claims to be. A sound reference means the disagreement was introduced downstream of it.

readings.name: Shape of the disagreement
readings.observed: scattered across channels, no single outlier
readings.purpose: Whether channels move together, one moves alone, or all scatter. Each fault leaves a different signature here.

readings.name: Apparent time against pulse height
readings.purpose: Whether large pulses appear earlier than small ones. A fixed threshold is crossed sooner by a steeper edge, which makes timing depend on amplitude rather than on physics.

readings.name: Measured cable lengths
readings.purpose: Physical path length per channel. Signal speed is finite, so extra cable is a fixed offset in one channel — measurable with a tape rather than a scope.

readings.name: Identical test pulses injected at the inputs
readings.purpose: Removes the detectors and the event, leaving the electronics and cable. Alignment here means the fixed delays through the chain are equal.

readings.name: Per-channel distribution width
readings.purpose: The spread of repeated measurements within one channel. A fixed error shifts a narrow distribution; a random one widens it.

title: Cable delay in a fast diagnostic
task: Estimate the time offset caused by unequal signal-cable lengths, then decide whether it should be corrected in hardware, calibration, or both.
scene: Two diagnostic channels observing the same fast event use cable paths that differ in length. The values are generic laboratory numbers: the point is to see how an ordinary physical length becomes a timing offset.
question: Estimate the time offset caused by unequal signal-cable lengths, then decide whether it should be corrected in hardware, calibration, or both.
takeaway: In a fast experiment, cable length is part of the timing model rather than invisible plumbing.
why: A signal traveling through a cable takes finite time, so unequal path length becomes unequal arrival time even when the sensors respond simultaneously. Divide the path difference by propagation speed to estimate the offset. The important metrology lesson is what comes next: either equalize paths or measure and correct the offsets, then verify the whole chain with a common pulse. Do not infer a physical asymmetry until the diagnostic asymmetry is smaller and better known than the effect being claimed.
assumes: a signal travels along a cable at a finite speed

title: Mechanical properties
task: Read the whole reading panel, including the calm readings, then select the one cause that fits all of it.
scene: A metal component from a non-nuclear test has cracked after a loading cycle, and the failure analysis has landed on your bench. The team has strength, stiffness, hardness, and toughness data, but only one of them addresses the observed failure mode directly.
question: Read the whole reading panel, including the calm readings, then select the one cause that fits all of it.
takeaway: Strength, stiffness, hardness, and toughness should not be treated as synonyms.
why: Four properties are involved and they are not synonyms. Elastic modulus is stiffness — how much it deflects under load. Yield strength is where permanent deformation begins. Hardness is resistance to indentation. Toughness is how much energy the material absorbs before it fractures. A material can be hard and brittle, or soft and very tough, so choosing the wrong one of these as 'strong' is how a part that passed every specification arrives cracked. A part is only as good as the property nobody inspected.
assumes: a material can be strong in one sense and weak in another

panel.title: The part that broke without bending
panel.hook: A machined component failed under a load it was qualified for. It broke cleanly, with no visible bending. The material certificate is in order and the part passed dimensional inspection before installation.
panel.riddle: The material was qualified for this load. What made this part different from the coupon that qualified it?

readings.name: Fracture surface appearance
readings.observed: flat cleavage facets, no shear lip
readings.reference: ductile tearing with a shear lip
readings.purpose: How the crack travelled. Cleavage means the material separated without absorbing much energy; it does not say why it was able to.

readings.name: Permanent deformation near the break
readings.reference: visible necking if the part yielded
readings.purpose: Whether the part deformed before it broke. Absence of deformation rules out simple overload past yield.

readings.name: Surface hardness vs bulk hardness
readings.purpose: Whether the outer layer differs from the interior. A hardened surface layer is often also a brittle one, and it can come from the material or from the machining.

readings.name: Crack origin location
readings.purpose: Where the failure started. A surface origin points at surface condition, geometry, or handling rather than at bulk material.

readings.name: Load history
readings.purpose: Whether the part was loaded once or repeatedly. Progressive cracking requires cycles; a single application does not produce it.

readings.name: Dimensions before failure
readings.purpose: Whether the part was made to size. In-tolerance dimensions remove geometry as the stress concentrator.

title: Why safety limits sit inside physical limits
task: A procedure sets conservative inventory, spacing, and handling limits well inside the calculated boundary. Why is that good laboratory design?
scene: Two radioactive-material operations are scheduled on the same bench. The written procedure uses conservative inventory and spacing controls rather than letting each shift calculate how close it thinks it can safely work.
question: A procedure sets conservative inventory, spacing, and handling limits well inside the calculated boundary. Why is that good laboratory design?
takeaway: A safety margin protects against uncertainty, changing configuration, and ordinary human error rather than expressing distrust of physics.
why: Administrative controls are intentionally more conservative than a calculated physical boundary because real laboratories have uncertainty, changing configurations, miscommunication, and multiple simultaneous errors. A written limit makes the safe state independent of who happens to be on shift and prevents a single mistake from consuming the entire margin. Historical criticality accidents at Los Alamos after the war reinforced this lesson dramatically. For the game, the player should reason about defense in depth—inventory control, spacing, independent checks, and stop-work authority—without calculating a weapon-relevant critical mass.
assumes: safe operation depends on configuration and uncertainty as well as a single nominal quantity

title: High-speed imaging and radiography
task: Estimate the blur distance.
scene: A non-nuclear materials experiment changes too quickly to inspect by eye. High-speed imaging and radiography are being used to measure motion inside an opaque test article without requiring a nuclear event.
question: Estimate the blur distance.
takeaway: A diagnostic is useful only if its spatial and temporal resolution are small compared with the feature being measured.
why: Motion during an exposure blurs a moving boundary by speed times exposure time. That makes resolution a quantitative question rather than a camera specification. If the blur is comparable to the feature of interest, the image cannot support a precise claim about that feature. High-speed optical and radiographic diagnostics were historically valuable because they turned very fast, partly hidden behavior into evidence. The senior-level lesson is to compare diagnostic resolution with the physical scale being inferred before trusting a beautiful image.
assumes: a photograph records everything that happened while the shutter was open

title: How timing error becomes position error
task: Estimate how far a fast front moves during the stated timing offset, then interpret that distance as a diagnostic-registration error.
scene: A surrogate fast-wave experiment is recorded by two channels that are offset by half a microsecond. Before diagnosing the physics, the team wants to know how much apparent spatial disagreement that timing error alone can create.
question: Estimate how far a fast front moves during the stated timing offset, then interpret that distance as a diagnostic-registration error.
takeaway: A timing error becomes a spatial error whenever the phenomenon being measured is moving.
why: For any moving front, distance equals speed times time. That converts an abstract timing mismatch into the amount of apparent spatial offset it can create in a measurement. Here the point is diagnostic: if a front moves several millimetres during the channel disagreement, two images or sensors can appear to describe different physics even when the event was identical. The correct response is to fix or calibrate the timing chain before treating the spatial difference as a property of the experiment.
assumes: a wave crosses a distance in a time set by its speed

title: Timing-module lot acceptance
task: Allocate 24 lot-test slots across the shipment so the plan can estimate the population distribution and tail without hand-picking champion units.
scene: A supplier has delivered a large lot of fast electrical timing modules used in the diagnostic system. One prototype looks excellent, but Bradbury wants evidence about the population the experiment will actually receive.
question: Allocate 24 lot-test slots across the shipment so the plan can estimate the population distribution and tail without hand-picking champion units.
takeaway: Reliability belongs to the manufactured population, so lot acceptance needs a representative distribution rather than a champion unit.
why: A prototype demonstrates that a design can work; it does not establish how a production lot behaves. If a fast experiment depends on many nominally identical timing modules, the tail of the distribution matters as much as the mean. Sample across the lot using a predefined plan, measure timing and failure behavior under the actual electrical conditions, and compare the distribution with an acceptance criterion written before the results are seen. This is generic manufacturing statistics and metrology, not explosive-component design.
assumes: a sample of a production run says something about the rest of it
why_this_format: The surgical pass reframes this as a manufactured-population problem under a fixed test budget. ALLOCATE turns that constraint into the reasoning: every repeat spent on the same attractive unit is a test not spent sampling another part of the lot. The player has to buy representative coverage of the population and its tail, not merely accumulate good-looking measurements.
player_does: distribute a fixed pool of test slots across early, middle, and late portions of the production lot
reserve enough tests for a representative stressed subset rather than only nominal-condition repeats
decide whether to forgo repeated testing of the best-looking prototype so the required population questions remain answerable
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented authoring numbers: the five available test blocks cost 30 slots against a pool of 24. The required distribution and tail questions need broad lot coverage, while the optional champion-repeatability question consumes six slots without helping either required answer.

protectedItems.label: Fixture and reference-pulse check
protectedItems.note: Always performed; it does not answer a population question by itself.

items.label: Representative subset under specified electrical stress

answers.label: Estimate the manufactured population center and spread
Check whether the population tail remains acceptable under representative conditions
Measure repeatability of the single best-looking module

answerText: Use the slots to sample across the lot and include a representative stressed subset. The plan should be able to estimate the population distribution and its tail; repeated measurements of the champion unit are the question the fixed budget is allowed to forgo.

failure_feedback.action: spending six slots repeating the best-looking module
failure_feedback.consequence: the plan measures one unit very precisely while leaving the manufactured population under-sampled
failure_feedback.line: I need the lot, not its champion.

title: Synchronizing many channels
task: Estimate sigma_total.
scene: Dozens of diagnostic channels share a time reference, but their delays come from cables, electronics, triggering, and registration. A budget that omits one contribution can make every local check pass while the combined evidence is still misaligned.
question: Estimate sigma_total.
takeaway: A timing budget must include every significant term in the measurement chain and distinguish shared offsets from independent uncertainty.
why: Independent timing uncertainties combine in quadrature when their errors are uncorrelated. That is different from a shared clock bias, which shifts many channels together and does not average away. The arithmetic therefore comes after the dependency map: decide which terms are independent, then combine those statistically and carry common-mode terms separately. The largest variance contribution is usually the best place to improve first. This is exactly the kind of systems reasoning an integrated diagnostic campaign requires.
assumes: independent errors do not simply add

dayTitle: Build an uncertainty and dependency budget
title: Carrying uncertainty through
task: Estimate the total fractional uncertainty.
scene: A predicted reaction rate rests on a cross section known to a few per cent and a flux known to a few more. Theory is being asked how well the prediction is known.
question: Estimate the total fractional uncertainty.
takeaway: Adding independent uncertainties linearly is usually too pessimistic; ignoring correlation can be too optimistic.
why: Independent uncertainties combine in quadrature when they are genuinely uncorrelated: square each contribution, add the squares, and take the square root. Eight percent and six percent therefore combine to ten percent, not fourteen. The larger term contributes more of the variance, so reducing it usually buys more improvement. But that arithmetic is valid only after checking independence. If both numbers share a calibration or model assumption, the common part must be carried as a correlated uncertainty rather than hidden inside the square root.
assumes: two independent errors are unlikely to be wrong the same way at once

dayTitle: Build an uncertainty and dependency budget
title: Where the fragments go
task: A nucleus at rest splits into a heavy and a light fragment. Which carries more kinetic energy?
scene: A nucleus initially at rest splits into a heavier and a lighter fragment. The total momentum must still sum to zero, and the group is arguing about which fragment therefore carries the larger share of the kinetic energy.
question: A nucleus at rest splits into a heavy and a light fragment. Which carries more kinetic energy?
takeaway: Momentum conservation fixes the ratio of fragment speeds, and energy follows from it.
why: The nucleus was at rest, so total momentum is zero and the fragments leave with equal and opposite momentum: the lighter one moves faster in inverse proportion to its mass. Kinetic energy is momentum squared over twice the mass, so with momenta equal the energies go as one over mass — the lighter fragment takes the larger share. Both conservation laws are doing separate work here, which is the point: momentum fixes the speeds, and energy then follows from them.
assumes: momentum is conserved in an isolated system

dayTitle: Build an uncertainty and dependency budget
title: Build the integrated diagnostic uncertainty budget
task: Use the reading panel to identify the two uncertainty sources that explain the anomalies without double-counting the shared calibration.
scene: A non-nuclear compression experiment has produced several anomalies. Some measurements share the same calibration chain, and the team has only enough time to improve one part of the evidence system before the next trial.
question: Use the reading panel to identify the two uncertainty sources that explain the anomalies without double-counting the shared calibration.
takeaway: The most useful improvement targets the dominant independent uncertainty, not the loudest anomalous number.
why: An uncertainty budget starts with a dependency map. Two measurements that use the same calibration, reconstruction model, or reference sample do not provide two independent constraints on that shared term. Once dependencies are explicit, the team can separate random spread, calibration bias, and model-form uncertainty and ask which one contributes most to the final claim. The correct next experiment is the one that attacks a dominant uncertainty with genuinely new information. More repetitions through the same bottleneck create confidence without independence.
assumes: two problems can have two different causes

panel.title: Two entries in one uncertainty budget
panel.hook: A non-nuclear compression trial has returned two problems: the timing channels arrived over a wider spread than budgeted, and the inferred peak density is below prediction. The budget has to name causes, and no single entry accounts for both.
panel.riddle: Which independent uncertainty sources account for the timing anomaly and the inference anomaly without counting one shared dependency twice?

readings.name: Channel arrival spread
readings.purpose: How closely the measurement channels agreed. A wide spread can come from hardware, path differences, or lot-to-lot propagation variation.

readings.name: Test-medium wave-speed certificates
readings.observed: spread of 2.4% across the lots used
readings.reference: within 0.5% for a single qualified lot
readings.purpose: Whether nominally equivalent test-medium lots propagate the disturbance consistently. Lot-to-lot variation can broaden channel arrival times.

readings.name: Sensor placement metrology
readings.purpose: Whether path-length differences were introduced by placement. In-tolerance metrology removes the simplest geometric explanation.

readings.name: Shared trigger self-test
readings.purpose: Whether the common timing reference fired when commanded. A common-trigger fault would move many channels together rather than create independent lot variation.

readings.name: Inferred peak density
readings.purpose: The result after converting the radiographic measurement into a physical quantity. It depends on both the raw data and the calibration model.

readings.name: Raw radiographic transmission
readings.purpose: The measurement before interpretation. Normal raw data with an abnormal inferred value points toward the conversion rather than the observation.

readings.name: Attenuation calibration against a step wedge
readings.purpose: Whether the model that turns transmission into inferred density is valid where it is being used. A high-density calibration failure biases the reported peak.

title: Acceptance criteria
task: Estimate the conservative lower bound of the measurement.
scene: A property has to be at least a hundred units and the measurement reads a hundred and two, plus or minus three. Material this scarce cannot be scrapped casually, or accepted on hope.
question: Estimate the conservative lower bound of the measurement.
takeaway: Acceptance criteria need explicit rules for uncertainty and borderline results.
why: An acceptance criterion needs a threshold, a measurement method, and a stated rule for uncertainty. Borderline results are exactly why the rule must be agreed before the number appears. Here the central value is 102, but the conservative lower bound is 99, below the required 100. That means the measurement does not demonstrate an unambiguous pass under this rule. Another organization could choose a different predeclared rule; the important lesson is that the decision rule should not change after the result is known.
assumes: a measurement has a range, not just a value

title: Instrumented non-nuclear tests
task: Spend the available facility week on the evidence that would most clearly separate the leading explanations for the unresolved behavior.
scene: Three test concepts are competing for one week of facility time. A non-nuclear test uses inert or surrogate material to reproduce motion, timing and shock behaviour without a chain reaction.
question: Spend the available facility week on the evidence that would most clearly separate the leading explanations for the unresolved behavior.
takeaway: The best test is the one whose possible outcomes discriminate among explanations, not the one that looks most like the final system.
why: A test earns facility time when its possible outcomes can change the program’s belief or next action. Before running it, ask what each leading explanation predicts. If both predict essentially the same measurement, that observable cannot distinguish them and the test buys little information. Choose the discriminating quantity first, then build the instrumentation around it. This reverses the common mistake of measuring whatever is easy and hoping the record becomes decisive afterward. A smaller test with distinct predictions can outperform a larger, more impressive but ambiguous one.
assumes: an experiment is worth what it can rule out
why_this_format: This stop is already about value of information: a smaller test can be more useful than a larger one if its possible outcomes separate the competing explanations. VALUE makes the player spend the scarce week explicitly. The winning purchase is not the most elaborate or statistically dense option; it is the test whose outcome can actually change which explanation remains viable.
player_does: inspect what each proposed test could measure and which competing explanation each result would support
spend a seven-day facility budget on one or more evidence options
commit the plan and see whether the purchased evidence can actually change the decision
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented authoring costs: the four options total 18 facility-days against a seven-day budget. The three-day discriminating test is decisive; the seven-day high-fidelity test uses the entire budget while both leading explanations predict essentially the same headline result.

options.label: Small test of the quantity on which the two hypotheses make different predictions
Largest available inert assembly with limited diagnostic access
Repeat one already-measured condition for tighter statistics
Repeat the previous configuration before its record is reconstructed

answerText: Buy the smaller test whose possible outcomes differ between the leading explanations. It uses less than the full facility week but produces information that can change the program’s belief; a larger ambiguous test or more repeats of the same condition do not.

failure_feedback.action: spending the whole week on the largest available test
failure_feedback.consequence: the record is expensive and high-fidelity, but both leading explanations predict the same headline outcome so the disagreement survives
failure_feedback.line: It can look more like the final system and still tell us less.

title: Critical path to an integrated trial
task: Estimate how much a parallel chain can slip before it controls the date.
scene: Three chains of work are running in parallel: diagnostic calibration, materials preparation, and facility readiness. The integrated trial cannot begin until all three finish, so the longest chain controls the date while the shorter chains carry schedule float.
question: Estimate how much a parallel chain can slip before it controls the date.
takeaway: Schedule management starts with dependencies, not activity counts.
why: The longest chain is the critical path. It is the only place where adding people or shifts moves the date. Effort poured into a task that is not on it changes nothing, however busy it makes everyone. It is spent on float that was already there. Float is the gap between the controlling chain and the one being worked on, and it is finite. Enough slippage on a parallel chain makes that chain the new critical path. At which point the whole calculation has to be done again.
assumes: work that can happen in parallel does not add up

title: What a scaled experiment can and cannot tell you
task: A smaller inert experiment is proposed. Decide which conclusions can transfer by similarity and which require full-scale validation.
scene: A smaller inert experiment could run in two weeks instead of six. The geometry is similar, but some material response times and diagnostic limits do not shrink with the model. The room is arguing about which conclusions are scale-independent.
question: A smaller inert experiment is proposed. Decide which conclusions can transfer by similarity and which require full-scale validation.
takeaway: A scaled experiment transfers only the behavior governed by the similarity conditions it actually preserves.
why: Scaled experiments are powerful when the dimensionless ratios that control a phenomenon are preserved. Geometric similarity by itself is not enough: fixed material timescales, diffusion lengths, sensor bandwidth, gravity, or rate-dependent constitutive behavior can break the analogy. Before running the model, write down which dimensionless groups are matched and which are not. Then restrict the conclusion to the physics those matched groups control. The senior-level lesson is disciplined inference from models, not any particular explosive scaling law.
assumes: a dimensionless ratio has the same value at any scale

title: What Trinity had to answer
task: Match each predeclared Trinity question to the kind of evidence that could answer it, including the safety-and-consequence question.
scene: The Trinity plan is being written as a set of questions before the event. There is one opportunity to collect integrated evidence, so each question needs a measurement path that can survive failure of another.
question: Match each predeclared Trinity question to the kind of evidence that could answer it, including the safety-and-consequence question.
takeaway: A full-system test is more informative when each question has its own evidence path before the event begins.
why: A test becomes vulnerable to hindsight if its questions are decided after the result. The Trinity teams needed evidence about integrated performance, the behavior of supporting systems, comparison with broad theoretical expectations, and radiological or physical effects. Those questions are not interchangeable and should not depend on one instrument. The deeper lesson is experimental design: predeclare what would count as evidence, arrange independent measurements where possible, and include consequences that matter to people beyond the technical team rather than treating them as external to the experiment.
assumes: a test proves what it was designed to ask

title: Field integration without losing the experiment
task: Arrange the field-integration steps so diagnostics, communications, weather, and safety systems are proven before the one-time event depends on them.
scene: The desert site has to function as a scientific field campaign: power, communications, weather observation, diagnostic stations, safety boundaries, and recovery plans all have to be ready before a one-time event can produce interpretable data.
question: Arrange the field-integration steps so diagnostics, communications, weather, and safety systems are proven before the one-time event depends on them.
takeaway: Field readiness means proving the support and evidence systems before the event makes them impossible to repair.
why: A one-time field experiment cannot be debugged after it has happened. Site services and communications come first because diagnostics and safety systems depend on them. Instruments are then calibrated and checked end-to-end while replacement is still possible. Weather and environmental monitoring must be tied to explicit hold or response criteria rather than being passive observations. Finally, the event proceeds only after independent readiness checks close the open interfaces. This preserves the systems-engineering lesson of Trinity without turning the sequence into a device-assembly procedure.
assumes: a schedule set by weather cannot be extended

title: The plot that makes a decay a straight line
task: How should the count-rate data be plotted, and what does the plot then give you?
scene: Two counters have produced a table of count rate against time, and the notebook has it plotted on ordinary axes as a curve that nobody can read a number off.
question: How should the count-rate data be plotted, and what does the plot then give you?
takeaway: Plotting a logarithm turns an exponential into a straight line, and its slope is the decay constant.
why: An exponential plotted on linear axes is a curve, and a curve is hard to read and harder to check. Take the logarithm of the count rate and the same data is a straight line whose slope is minus the decay constant — so the half-life comes out of a ruler rather than a guess. It also makes the failures visible: a second component appears as a break in slope, and background appears as the line flattening onto a floor. Choosing the axes is part of the measurement.
assumes: a logarithm turns a constant ratio into a constant difference

title: Where the energy in fission comes from
task: Why does splitting uranium release energy while splitting carbon would absorb it?
scene: A visitor asks why splitting a heavy nucleus releases energy while splitting a light one costs energy. The blackboard has the binding-energy curve on it and nobody has used it to answer.
question: Why does splitting uranium release energy while splitting carbon would absorb it?
takeaway: The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve says which way a nuclear reaction releases energy.
why: Binding energy per nucleon rises steeply from hydrogen, peaks around iron and nickel, and falls slowly to uranium. A reaction releases energy when its products sit HIGHER on that curve than its reactants, because the products are more tightly bound. Uranium splitting into two mid-mass fragments moves up the curve, so energy comes out. Carbon splitting would move down it, so energy would have to go in. The same curve is why fusion of light nuclei also releases energy — from the other side of the peak.
assumes: a nucleus is held together by binding energy

dayTitle: Reconcile evidence and freeze the design
title: Compare a prediction band with an observation
task: Estimate the offset in units of the measurement uncertainty, then state the strongest justified conclusion.
scene: A model predicts an observable between fifteen and twenty-five units. The measurement reads twenty-one, plus or minus two. The temptation after Trinity is to read one comparison as a verdict on everything.
question: Estimate the offset in units of the measurement uncertainty, then state the strongest justified conclusion.
takeaway: Evidence should update a model claim by claim, not by declaring total victory.
why: The gap between an observation and a prediction is measured in units of the measurement's own uncertainty. Take the difference and divide by that uncertainty. Half a sigma from the middle of the band is consistent. But consistency with a band this wide is weak evidence, because fifteen to twenty-five would have accommodated almost anything. Agreement supports the part of the model that produced the band, and no more. One agreeing diagnostic can sit beside others that disagree, and those still need explaining.
assumes: a wide prediction is easy to agree with

dayTitle: Reconcile evidence and freeze the design
title: Why isotope separation is physically difficult
task: Explain why ordinary chemistry has little leverage for separating two isotopes of the same element, without turning the answer into an enrichment-process recipe.
scene: A chemistry group is asked why ordinary reagents cannot simply pull uranium-235 away from uranium-238. The useful senior-level answer lies in what electrons know—and do not know—about the nucleus.
question: Explain why ordinary chemistry has little leverage for separating two isotopes of the same element, without turning the answer into an enrichment-process recipe.
takeaway: Isotopes have nearly the same chemistry because they share electron structure; separation must exploit small physical differences such as mass.
why: Chemical behavior is controlled mainly by electrons, and isotopes of the same element have essentially the same electron structure. Their main difference is nuclear mass, so ordinary chemistry offers very little selectivity. Historically, Manhattan Project enrichment technologies therefore exploited small mass-dependent physical effects and required enormous industrial effort. For this course, that is the important concept: a tiny fractional mass difference must be amplified through engineering. The lesson should stop at the principle rather than reproduce the operating details of enrichment technologies.
assumes: chemical behaviour is set by electrons, and isotopes differ only in the nucleus

dayTitle: Reconcile evidence and freeze the design
title: Theory-experiment reconciliation
task: Spend 100 investigation credits on the next evidence. Buy what can distinguish a shared calibration problem from a missing physical effect.
scene: Theory and experiment disagree by three standard deviations and the division has to decide what to do about it. Arguing about which explanation is right is cheaper than finding out, and worth less.
question: Spend 100 investigation credits on the next evidence. Buy what can distinguish a shared calibration problem from a missing physical effect.
takeaway: A discrepancy is most useful when the next measurement is designed to make competing explanations predict different outcomes.
why: Two numbers that share a calibration can be three sigma apart because one error was counted twice. The audit is cheap enough to do first. What has to follow it is a measurement whose outcome differs depending on which explanation is true. A detector artefact, a missing physical effect, or an approximation pushed past its range all predict different things. Design the test that separates them, and spend the credits there rather than on the one that reassures.
assumes: three standard deviations is a real disagreement, not noise
why_this_format: The updated stop says the next measurement should make the competing explanations predict different outcomes, and explicitly warns against spending credits on reassurance. VALUE is therefore a direct fit. The player must distinguish an audit that checks a shared dependency from more data that reuse it, and then buy genuinely independent evidence rather than forcing the model to agree by retuning parameters.
player_does: inspect the dependency axis and the physical-prediction axis for each proposed investigation
spend a fixed credit budget on the audit or measurement package that could separate the explanations
commit the evidence plan before seeing which explanation it favors
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented authoring costs: the board costs 170 credits against a 100-credit budget. The combined calibration audit plus independent-chain discriminating measurement costs 75 and is decisive; cheaper model retuning and same-chain repeats cannot distinguish the explanations.

options.label: Audit the shared calibration, then measure the discriminating observable through an independent chain
Collect more measurements through the same calibration and analysis chain
Retune uncertain model parameters until the current measurement is reproduced

answerText: Audit the shared calibration and then make a measurement through an independent chain whose prediction differs between the competing explanations. More same-chain data can narrow the wrong answer, and parameter retuning can hide the discrepancy without explaining it.

failure_feedback.action: buying more measurements through the same calibration chain
failure_feedback.consequence: the statistical error shrinks while any shared calibration bias remains in every new point
failure_feedback.line: More of the same dependency is not independent evidence.

dayTitle: Reconcile evidence and freeze the design
title: Post-Trinity design freeze
task: Arrange the four cards from earliest cause or prerequisite to latest result.
scene: Trinity has produced new evidence and there is almost no time to use it. The pressure at this moment is to keep improving, and every unlogged improvement breaks the link between the test and the article.
question: Arrange the four cards from earliest cause or prerequisite to latest result.
takeaway: A freeze comes before the paperwork, or the paperwork describes something still changing.
why: Each stage is the input to the next. The timing, hydrodynamic and radiation records are reconciled into one account of the shot, because there is nothing to compare until they agree with each other. That account is then compared with the pre-test predictions, and what remains unexplained is named rather than absorbed. Only then can the evidence-supported changes be approved and the configuration frozen. The freeze comes before the paperwork — reverse those two and the documents describe a configuration that is still moving.
assumes: what was tested and what gets built can drift apart

dayTitle: Complete the evidence chain—and confront responsibility
title: Why light nuclei release energy too
task: Use the binding-energy curve to explain why both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei can release energy, then separate energy release from practical feasibility.
scene: The binding-energy curve rises from light nuclei toward iron and falls toward very heavy nuclei. A student asks why movement toward the peak can release energy from either side, and why that does not mean every such reaction is easy to produce.
question: Use the binding-energy curve to explain why both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei can release energy, then separate energy release from practical feasibility.
takeaway: The binding-energy curve explains energetic direction; reaction barriers and probabilities determine whether a process is easy to realize.
why: Products that are more tightly bound per nucleon than their reactants have lower total mass-energy, so the difference can appear as released energy. Heavy-nucleus fission and light-nucleus fusion can both move products toward the peak of the binding-energy curve. That does not make the processes equally accessible: charged nuclei repel one another, while neutron-induced reactions face different barriers and probabilities. The senior-level lesson is to separate thermodynamic possibility from kinetic or interaction-rate feasibility.
assumes: like charges repel, and the nuclear force acts only at very short range

dayTitle: Complete the evidence chain—and confront responsibility
title: Final diagnostic readiness review
task: You can independently verify only two readiness claims. Choose which claims to verify before approving deployment.
scene: The final readiness review asks whether the experiment’s instruments can produce trustworthy evidence under a one-time event. A sensor that saturates, loses timing, or shares a hidden dependency with its backup can erase an entire conclusion.
question: You can independently verify only two readiness claims. Choose which claims to verify before approving deployment.
takeaway: Diagnostic readiness means knowing how evidence can fail and arranging independent ways to recognize that failure.
why: Calibration and configuration records come first. An instrument nobody can describe afterwards produces data nobody can use. End-to-end timing and health checks then prove the chain works as a chain, rather than as a set of working parts. Independent coverage of the critical observables comes next — independent, so one failure does not take a whole answer with it. Deployment is approved with the residual risks named and a backup for each. Readiness means failures will be recognised, not that there are none.
assumes: an instrument can be working and still miss the event
why_this_format: The surgical pass defines readiness as knowing how evidence can fail, not merely collecting signed records. ATTEST makes that distinction physical: the board contains claims that look complete, but the verification budget cannot cover all of them. The player must spend scarce checks on critical claims that lack independent backing rather than rechecking paperwork that already has evidence behind it.
player_does: review the signed readiness claims and the evidence already attached to each one
spend two independent verification checks on the claims whose failure could erase a critical conclusion
approve or refuse deployment after the verification outcomes are revealed
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented authoring claims and budget: there are five claims but only two verification checks. One critical calibration/configuration claim is already independently backed, while the critical end-to-end timing and independence claims are unbacked and both fit within the two-check budget.

claims.label: Calibration and configuration records match the deployed instruments
claims.verification: serial numbers, settings, and reference records agree

claims.label: The complete timing and health chain works at the required signal range
claims.verification: full-chain check exposes one channel that clips at the upper test amplitude

claims.label: Backup coverage is genuinely independent of the primary chain
claims.verification: dependency audit shows two nominal backups still share one timing reference

claims.label: The data archive and configuration log can be recovered
A spare sensor is staged at the field site

answerText: Spend the two independent checks on the critical claims that have no backing: the end-to-end timing/health chain and the independence of the backup coverage. A signature or completed record is not the physical condition, while the calibration/configuration claim already has independent evidence behind it.

failure_feedback.action: using a scarce verification on a critical claim that is already independently backed
failure_feedback.consequence: an unbacked end-to-end or independence failure can remain hidden even though the review folder looks more complete
failure_feedback.line: The record is not the condition. Spend the check where the condition is still unproven.

dayTitle: Complete the evidence chain—and confront responsibility
title: Final chemistry and metallurgy dossier
task: One last improvement to the division’s materials capability. Which?
scene: The final dossier has to show more than that components existed. The division has one last hundred credits of improvement to spend, and the choice says what it thinks a materials capability is.
question: One last improvement to the division’s materials capability. Which?
takeaway: A durable materials capability connects process history, measured structure, properties, uncertainty, and traceability.
why: A measurement describes one batch on one day. A durable materials capability connects process conditions, composition, structure, measured properties, uncertainty, and traceability across many batches. That is a stronger claim because it lets a later team diagnose why one lot differs from another instead of merely noticing that it does. It also exposes whether a property shift follows chemistry, heat treatment, handling, or measurement drift. The final dossier should therefore preserve relationships and provenance, not simply collect successful certificates.
assumes: somebody will read this after everyone who made it has gone

dayTitle: Complete the evidence chain—and confront responsibility
title: Scientific responsibility after Trinity
task: Separate the claims science can support from the political and ethical decisions it cannot make by itself, then decide what information scientists still have a duty to put on the record.
scene: Trinity has demonstrated an unprecedented destructive scale, nearby communities were not warned about fallout, and debate inside the project is growing. The Szilard petition has gathered more than fifty signatures elsewhere, while the Franck Report argues for international control and consideration of a demonstration.
question: Separate the claims science can support from the political and ethical decisions it cannot make by itself, then decide what information scientists still have a duty to put on the record.
takeaway: Expertise does not grant political authority, but it creates a responsibility to state consequences, uncertainty, and foreseeable harms clearly.
why: Scientists possess technical knowledge that decision-makers and the public may not have: what was measured, what remains uncertain, what physical effects are plausible, and where the evidence is weak. That does not give scientists sole authority over war or diplomacy. It does create a responsibility to state consequences and uncertainty clearly rather than hiding them behind expertise or secrecy. A complete history must also include people outside the laboratory—downwind communities and families displaced from project lands—because the consequences of technical work do not stop at the project boundary.
assumes: a technical question and a decision about its use are different questions
